title: The English and Romanian Adoptees
text:
In the early 1990s, many British families adopted children from Romanian orphanages, where conditions had been extremely poor. The child psychiatrist Michael Rutter and his team at the Institute of Psychiatry in London saw a rare chance to learn how far children can recover from severe early deprivation. They began following 111 Romanian children adopted into English homes before the age of two, and compared them with children born and adopted within Britain.

When they arrived, many of the Romanian children were badly underweight, small for their age and far behind in development. By age four, the picture had changed dramatically. Physical growth had largely caught up, and so had much of their cognitive development.

The age at adoption made a clear difference. Children who had left the orphanage before about six months of age did about as well as the British-born adoptees. Those adopted later had, on average, lower scores, even though they too had made large gains. The team kept following the children into adolescence and adulthood, and found that some difficulties linked to longer deprivation persisted for a minority.

The study showed both sides of the story: how resilient young children are when given a loving home, and how much time in deprivation can cost.
lesson: Love and a stable home can repair a great deal, and the sooner a child gets them the better. Never assume a child is beyond help.
people: Michael Rutter and the English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) Study Team
source: Rutter, M., and the English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) Study Team (1998). Developmental catch-up, and deficit, following adoption after severe global early privation. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 39(4), 465-476.
place: Institute of Psychiatry, Denmark Hill, London, England
